title: Touching Earth Sangha
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett and Satya
summary: The talk's main teaching is that true wisdom can be cultivated by embracing uncertainty and discomfort, rather than relying on expertise or rightness. This approach involves taking on roles without a basis in personal expertise, allowing for comfort with the unknown, and finding wisdom through experiential learning and simple living. By practicing this type of wisdom, individuals can develop a deeper understanding of themselves and the world around them, leading to a more authentic and compassionate way of life.

Speaker labels mark the handovers the recording makes clear.

**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Good evening everybody.
Thank you for being here.
I was thinking, we've been studying for the last month or so wisdom, Mahayana Buddhist teachings on wisdom, through the sutras on prajna paramita, which we chant about a lot as well.
One of the ways of looking at wisdom is from the point of view of a conventional, self-oriented basis.
Often when we think about wisdom, we think about expertise, we think about doing it right, we think about avoiding embarrassment, actually.

And the prajna paramita teachings seem to be suggesting there's another kind of wisdom, or a deeper wisdom, or a fuller wisdom, where the basis is not to be an expert, or to be right, or to know something.
I was thinking we have various ways to enact that in our practice.
The learning about prajna paramita is fundamentally experiential.
The learning about this wisdom that doesn't have a basis in any of those things, or doesn't have a basis at all, is one of the ways this is expressed.
Wisdom with no basis whatsoever, just wisdom.

We've talked many times about how we've inherited a somewhat complex ritual form, and the people doing the different roles in that ritual form are not necessarily the experts, which would be a rational thing from a usual wisdom point of view.
You would train up your best bell ringer and use him until he dies, which I guess we kind of did tonight, because John has done this how many thousands of times?
Hopefully I have a few more years.
Luckily you're still making mistakes, so we're okay.
We put ourselves in these positions not really knowing what we're doing, so the basis of our activity is not being the expert or getting it right, but just the doing of it.
There's some richness in there, and of course psychologically that gives us various problems.
We can feel anxious, we can feel self-conscious, we can feel like we don't know enough, but over time we develop a certain comfort with that.
There's something comfortable about that kind of discomfort, something that's beyond our personal constricted sense of wanting to look good, or at least not look bad, wanting to blend in maybe.
These kinds of roles that we have in Zen practice prevent us from blending in.
Have you noticed that?
They make people stick out.
And it goes all the way through all the roles, as we've often said.
Even the person giving the talk is not giving the talk because they're the best trained person to give the talk.
They're giving the talk because that's their job.

And I was thinking, in our rituals of private interview, our way of practicing this wisdom without a basis: currently in our practice [unclear: "mail you"], you can see me and you can see five other teachers.
The other folks you have to sign up for, which is the only difference really.
But to show up in that interview not knowing really what you're going to say.
You could of course rehearse something and think that you have some basis for being there, right?
Some reason why you're there.
Some question you want answered.
You could think that that's true, and if that gets you there, that's great.
Skillful means.
Once you're there, little by little you find out: that's not why I'm here.
That's not why I'm here.
Together with the teacher you can explore a conversation that doesn't have a basis, somehow beyond the limits of personality.
Sometimes we touch this, other times we just have a chat about something, and that's okay.
Even then.
And we can do activities for multiple days to help us by pulling away the basis.
One of our usual bases is our habitual activity, right?
The things we do to keep ourselves entertained and reassured and so on.
Nothing wrong with these things, but it's interesting from time to time to take all that away.
So Bob, it's wonderful to have Bob back. [unclear: "Raise on Bob"].
Mountain spirit Bob.
Back from the mountains, and doing the 11 day hiking. 12 days of hiking.
Much of the usual basis of the activity of the hikers was not there.
Some things were there.
Their bodies were still there.
But very few of their usual comfort-seeking activities were available.
And apparently towards the end when it was like 30 degrees, raining, the basis can fall away.
So that's a wonderful practice, and we practice multi-day meditation retreats.
One of the great powers there is the schedule for practicing wisdom without a basis.
One of our most powerful bases is deciding what we get to do.
Of course we don't all get to decide what we get to do all the time.
We have to go to work or whatever it is.
But even then we're still in sneaky little ways exercising our choices and our desires.
So it's interesting to be on a meditation retreat with a very strong schedule.
You don't get to choose very much.
They choose the food, they choose when you wake up, when you go to bed.
They choose whether you're standing or sitting or walking or lying down.
And one of the ways Buddha described our life is that that's actually all that's happening.
It's one of those four things.
There's nothing else to do: either sitting, standing, lying or walking.
We have so many complicated things we have to do, and it actually boils down to that.
Or one could take on a life with fewer bases, fewer conventional bases, for a long time.
A whole lifetime.
So these are ways perhaps of practicing the Prajnaparamita teachings.
Seeing for ourselves what's the feeling of this.
What's the feeling of stopping something for a while or taking something else up for a while.
Or going into a situation where I don't feel comfortable.
I don't feel like I have expertise or assuredness or authority.
Just to see what happens.
I've been enjoying it.
I haven't got to spend as much time with them as I would like.
We've had three sangha guests, and Al Boris has been helping them with the roof.
We've been providing them a place to sit still and do nothing.
That's our great offering.
And they are members of what's it called?
Touching Earth.
Touching Earth Sangha.
And they have [unclear: "consulated"] an interesting way of practicing with less of a conventional basis, and I'm curious to hear a little bit about it.
So I thought we would invite Satya to speak a little bit.
And maybe Fallon and Andy would like to add something, if something is to be added.
And maybe you don't have to have someone behind you.
Satya, if you don't mind, you can come up here.
Can you handle these inflatable things?
Yeah, I feel this.
To maximize my comfort.
Yeah, well you won't have a good basis for sitting there.
Yeah, solid.
This is my favorite.
My favorite Satya.
Rolled up sweater.
Tried many different kinds.
This is in a bicycle seat.
Chronic.
Legs falling asleep.
Something like that you might try.
Thanks for being here.
Thanks for coming up.
So you folks are living in a pretty simple way, I think.
With no money.
Very little money.
Simple food.
Simple activities.
So what do you do?
And how did you come by that way of practicing?
**Satya:** It's interesting, this word simplicity.
I use it all the time.
I advocate simple living.
I sometimes describe ourselves as living simply.
But sometimes I think about that.
It's not necessarily any more simple than in other people's lives.
In some ways, I don't pay bills and taxes, and maybe there's less paperwork.
But like the Buddha said, we have sitting, lying down, walking.
We're doing the same things, and we have decisions to make and things to think about.
Sure, it's simpler, but it's different in some ways.
At least it looks that way.
I started practice at some usual Zen centers, or more conventional than what I'm doing now.
Some of you have heard of them: Berkeley Zen Center and Tassajara.
Also some smaller ones called Koji and Hokoji.
And [unclear: "Kobachino Roshi"] is my ordination teacher.
I had a lot of energy, especially at that time, for vigorous traditional-looking practice, so I wanted to go a little more traditional.
I went to Asia and I trained in Japan, mostly in Japan, and a little bit in Korea and China as well.
So many years in Zen centers or Asian temples.
In all those places you don't really have to have money, but I was determined to get used to this alternate life realm.

When I came back to the States in 2000, I aspired to continue that spirit of renunciate lifestyle, which of course is the original style of the Buddha and the vast majority of the well-known ancestors that we know.
It's not quite the same as wanting to follow the orthodox Vinaya, if you know what that is, all the rules.
To me, I was mostly interested in this spirit of investigating what a non-harming life is talked about as being.
Being very careful about your activities, that they don't harm other beings, and hopefully you actually find activities that help other beings.
That was true even at that time.
And I've always felt, growing up in this late industrial or post-industrial culture, there's more reason to be very careful about how we harm the rest of the world.
Because actually, if we investigate our very normal actions now, we find their daily regular actions have quite an impact on the world.
Often negative.
The things we buy, they're disposable.
Driving our cars and using a lot of energy.
And we know that there's all kinds of environmental problems now.
So it seemed to me there's more reason to return to this model that the Buddha was trying to show in his early followers.
He was never adamant that everyone practice the same way.
He taught different people in different styles.
But he felt it was important that somebody is modeling how simple you can be and still have a very joyful life.
You still get to see that in some Asian countries.
If you've traveled to India you can see sadhus on the side of the road, and they're actually honored.
They're chosen to be homeless especially.
It's very beautiful.
People give them offerings.
In our country you see someone homeless and it's, oh, that's very pathetic.
How can I help?
Or I just ignore them.
It's very nice if you can say, how can I help?
But I grew up in New York City, and so many of you actually have to ignore them or you're spending all your time.

So I thought it would be very helpful in our culture if we had some models of people living simply, trying to be very careful and aware of the impacts of our daily decisions on other beings, human and otherwise, and the natural environment as a whole.
I guess I should say that I've always felt my first inspiration, as maybe many of you, to spiritual practice had something to do with an experience in nature or apprehending something in nature.
I did a lot of camping and hiking when I was quite young.
That was my first feeling that there's something beyond our stories that we tell to each other and our kind of goals and hopes and competitiveness and comparing and all that stuff.
Something that goes beyond all that, and a little more visible maybe in natural surroundings, at least for some people.
So that made me more sensitive maybe to wanting to live in a way that was least harming.
When I got back to the States, it's not as easy as in set up cultural situations in Asia.
But I found it not so hard physically to live with very little money or no money.
I don't make income.
I haven't since 1991.
Except gifts.
People give sometimes, and I try to give what I can as a gift as well.
Some of you might know this movement growing out of gift economy, a little different from barter actually.
You don't hold your offering until you get your matching, comparing if you're going to get enough exchange.
You just give, and you trust that nature will take care of returning what you need.
This is the kind of model I was trying to use.
I got involved in a group called Food Not Bombs.
There's a chapter here in Bellingham.
I'm not sure how active it is at the moment.
We gather food that would go to waste, and someone lets their kitchen be used.
We make a meal and bring it to a park.
We serve it to anyone who wants.
They can be poor and homeless, but they can also have a job and not be poor.
They just want to have community and share food.
Through offering in that way, and offering meditation instruction and [unclear: "touching instruction"], you get involved in the community and the community starts to offer some things.
Even though we grew up in a culture that doesn't understand that way so much, maybe it's somewhere in our subconscious, but still it works.
Some things are harder.
Some social things are harder.
People don't understand it.
I don't understand it actually.
A lot of people are attracted to it and don't understand it.
Other people are repelled by it and don't understand it.
We've had a sangha that meets once a week, and we meet whenever we can, whenever it's offered.
We don't have our own place.
For a little while someone gave a lot of money all of a sudden, so we rented a place for a while.
That's when it came up.
Then the landlord wanted to sell it.
It was summer.
We thought we could have outside for a while, and then various people started to drift away pretty quickly.
A little later we found a free house that someone let us use.
That had its limits.
For a while we had a residential place.
We've been meeting on Sundays for a long time.
Then Fallon and Andy have been practicing with me.
Fallon first practiced with me a couple of years ago.
He's been in [unclear: "Great Vow's end center"] a little bit.
And Andy I met just about a year ago.
For a three summer we decided to take this bike trip, because we don't use cars.
So we bike from Portland through Western Washington, looking to see if we can make connections and see if some land appears that we might have as a residential place.
Very simply, and grow some food.
But to be able to have a place that we can invite people to.
That's something that we haven't been able to have.
And offer retreats or donation, which is the way that I receive them, for workshops and hopefully food.
And see how that experiment would work.
So that's why we're on this trip.
To relate to the prajna or prajna.
We're all practitioners of whatever sort that we are.

However much we're challenging our conventional lifestyle, when you're touching beyond our understanding, our thinking, our conventions, I feel it's very important that we take whatever inspiration we get from that.
Meaning when we discover the satisfaction of just being alive.
Of just being present.
The satisfaction before our ideas of the goals, and the satisfaction of pleasures that we think we want.
All those things that conventionally people go after. [unclear: "Girls love money"], relationship.
Status.
Whatever it might be.
*[Nomon Tim Burnett and Satya share this talk.

Spiritual level we have.
Enlightenment.
Pretty much enlightenment.
That's what we focus on, whatever that might be.
But we touch this place where there's something underneath all that, just as a miracle of being alive.
So for me, the next step, and I think probably for all of us, is: how do we bring that inspiration to save all beings from suffering?
That's the word we like to use.
Of course we don't even know what "all beings" means, but something in our heart maybe knows about that.

So to me, choosing a life that's kind of not participating in some things that aren't necessarily unwholesome, but often lead to unwholesomeness: the pursuit of money, the pursuit of status, the use of a lot of resources, the pursuit of a high level of comfort and budget.
That is one way of expressing the inspiration that just being alive is content.
If that's so, we can really recreate our life.
We have an empty field to experiment.
So maybe we experiment and it ends up looking pretty similar to what we were doing before.
That might be the [unclear: "real hard expression"] of some people.
And for others of us, it's to clear the field and start fresh.
We say, "Hey, I want this, this is more joyful.
I think this is a greater offering to the world.
This is more beautiful than what I was doing before."
That freedom to be able to find a new way is, to me, one of the great gifts of our practice.
When we find that we don't need what we thought we needed, and just being alive is enough, we touch that place in zazen or in chanting or whatever our practice involves.
We say, "How can I carry that out into my life every moment?
How can I now bring that question to my job, my relationships, my family?
If I don't have to go on any of my habits because just being here is enough, how will my expression be?
How can I create the most beautiful expression for all beings?"
So this is what I've come up with so far.
Work in progress.
Meet other practitioners in general.
It's very wonderful to meet other people.
Some people are put off by some things we're doing.
A lot of people are supportive.
Some people are confused.
But it's usually a pretty rich meeting.
It's traveling, although it's quite difficult.
I've done a lot of traveling in my life and I think I more enjoy not traveling these days.
So it has its challenges, and it has these great rewards of touching people in different places and taking us outside of our usual social group.
I think it's very rich and fertile.

People learn about our expression and we learn about other people's spiritual expression, and hopefully it helps to create something very deep as an expression of our practice in this country, in this culture, in this time.
I hope something very relevant in addressing the issues we have in the world now, which to me seem, at least in the relative world, dominated by this very serious psychological crisis.
We find the true meaning of this word "responsibility," our true responsibility, meaning our true ability to respond to the situation, to not deny anything, to not hide anything.
We really see what it is, how we participate in it, and what we might do to free ourselves and free other beings.
So sometimes people tell me, "This seems too extreme or too radical, what you're doing."
And I recognize sometimes the big difference in how other people are living.
But of course it doesn't seem that way to me. [unclear: "All of our life passed, but it doesn't seem radical to anybody."] But contrasted with the right things, it's a discovery.
I'm very grateful that Tim responded very open-heartedly from the first time I contacted him.
We were in Port Townsend, that was another place we were looking at, Olympia.
One of the most hospitable towns in Western Washington.
We were picking out places to start, and we wanted to give ourselves too much challenge.
And Alvarez has been very kind, giving us a place to stay.
What kinds of things are the sort of core agreements in terms of the lifestyle with the three of you?
So money, diet, what else?
We never set it out very strictly.
I guess if we have a bigger group one day we'll have to actually put guidelines on the walls.
And it's always good to bring up.
We question these things and sometimes change them.
But what I found, and I think mostly Falon and Andy are in agreement on so far, is we're trying not to use fossil fuels.
We're trying basically not to use money.
We're not very strict about that, because I feel it's very important to receive gifts, and that's a big part of traditional Buddhist practice.
When I was training in a monastery in Japan we did Takahatsu, it's called in Japan, [unclear: "moms collecting rounds"].

Which is a really, really interesting practice, particularly challenging for Westerners, because we've kind of grown up with this capitalist system where everyone is an individual and makes your own way, you're not dependent on anyone else.
So it's kind of demeaning or something, or it's very difficult for people to ask for offerings.

And like I said before, our only example of impoverished people are people that we feel have failed, and often they feel they've failed, and they're maybe alcoholic or something, so it's kind of degrading.
But in this older tradition, starting with the Buddha, actually probably started before the Buddha, but the Buddha being an example, it's very noble to actually ask for offerings.
This is very challenging to our culture.

But I had that experience in Japan where, although it's a dying tradition, our temple did Takahatsu, and it was really very, very interesting to see the reactions of people, both people who are not used to it, young people, totally surprised, and old people who haven't seen it for decades, and they're so honoring, old women getting on their knees, in fact.
You just feel like, "I'm not worthy of this."
It's a really wonderful experience.
So...
So receiving money.
Yeah, sorry.

So we receive money, and we pretty much only use it for, we get a lot of our food for free, but sometimes to keep healthy we need to buy some things that are hard to come by, grains mostly, and not much else.
But I have a good friend who is a spiritual practitioner also.

His name is Suelo, he goes by Suelo, or Daniel, and his practice forms live very strictly without money, so he refuses it if it's offered to him, and if someone sneaks it to him, which happens quite a bit, sneaks it in the back pocket or something, he has to spend it by midnight that night.
Which actually echoes the Buddha's idea.
Of course, traditional monks don't touch money at all, but even with food, you can't save it for the next day, because you get this hoarding thing.
Yeah, I know what that's like.
You pay $100 and they're like, "Oh, we've got to hoard this and save it for the best opportunity."
So he lives that way.
Someone wrote a book about him, *The Man Who Quit Money*, that's quite interesting.
You can probably find it in the [unclear: "book stories"] here.
But we receive money and use it somewhat, and our food, we try to eat what we feel is the least harming diet, which is no animal products.

I started vegetarian first, and then I learned that dairy and eggs generally come from animals that are also killed pretty quickly after their most productive years, and dairy calves are ripped from their dairy mothers, and the cows are kept pregnant all the time, so there's a lot of killing still involved.
Of course, the more you get away from commercial situations, with eggs and in other ways, the less suffering.
So we just avoid animal products, and we avoid packaging too.
I got educated about plastic and the problems of that, I'm sure a lot of you know.
Some of that, especially in the ocean, but really all over the world, it's becoming incredibly ubiquitous.
So we just don't use plastic packaging anymore.
It's kind of an experiment.
When you learn something has unwholesome results, the question for me is, well, can we live without it?
Some things that are so common about plastic, it seems like we can't, but I found that if you really have strong intention to get used to new sets of habits, it's not so hard.
It really helps to have a co-op or a natural food store with bulk food, of course.
So we use bags, I'm sure you all do that sometimes too, and fill up with bulk food, but we just won't buy stuff in this way with plastic.
And what else would you, you guys want to add something?
How about, this is a lot of things that you avoid, but how about the doing, yeah, the doing, I mean, a daily schedule?

Right, of course, we have retreats sometimes, seven-day retreats, like you mentioned, and we really aspire to have three-month practice periods, if we have a place for that, if we can secure such a long time.
That's the kind of older tradition in Korea and China, at least: a three-month summer retreat and then a three-month winter retreat, and in between any traveling time.
So it's an interesting model to me.
When we're on retreat, we have a pretty conventional schedule, I think, [unclear: "then schedule, I think, precision"].
For traveling, it all gets very flexible, but at least we always sit in the morning for about an hour, and we do also Qigong and Tai Chi, moving kinds of meditation.
And we also do a music practice, which is kind of like a chanting practice, from a tradition of Indian singing, Indian music called Raga.
And if we're not traveling, we spend a lot of time gathering free food, working with food outposts to offer meals to people.
Occasionally I give talks and classes and things.
What else do you do?
Oh yeah, we do wilderness trips.
I've heard about you and your trips, so we also lead those kinds of things.
We were based in Portland, so we would go out to Mt.
Hood, and of course, because we were trying not to use fossil fuels, we do it all by bicycle.
We put our backpacks on the back rack, and it's new to a lot of people.
We built our own stoves that use little twigs so we don't have to use gas for them.
So we introduce people to new ways of backpacking, which is a little unusual.
And of course, we sit during the backpacking, but we don't have a very strict schedule.
In the evening we sit again, music practice if we can, we do two or three times a day, and Tai Chi and Qigong two times a day.
Actually, practice takes up a lot of the day.
Practice and mundane errands to gather the food is most of the time.
If we had a place that was a little more stable, we'd have more time to offer retreats and workshops.
We also get involved in activism sometimes, protests and things like that, but that's not very regular.
And then there's email.
Of course, we do use email.
Tai Chi takes an awful lot of time.
Has anyone had any, if we had any more time?
We have a minute or two, but not too long.
And you're leaving us tomorrow, I should imagine, if you want to be in Seattle.
Yeah, there's a conference on Saturday.
I was thinking that's 90 miles away, so I might need to...
Yeah, it's actually very auspicious.
On the bike routes, it's 108 miles.
Oh yeah?
It's coming up all the time for me recently.
I was just looking at a farm that we might go visit, and it's 108 acres.
I was just like, what's happening?
That's a special number, if you don't know.
The length of a [unclear: "bomb"].
Right.
A number of different kinds of delusions and transformations.
How do you get your email?
Well, for a long time we just used computers in libraries, but there's a non-profit computer place in Portland.
They take old computers, recycle them and rebuild them, and they give away computers to politicians, non-profits.

So I was a little intimidated because we're not really a non-profit or anything, but when we had a little larger number of people living together, I applied and they're like, "Oh yeah, we've got lots," and we got two laptops.
But of course we have to find a place that has internet.
That part's pretty conventional.
We don't have phones, so in this day and age, without phones or a computer, you'd be pretty hard to reach, especially if you don't have a place with phones.
We'd like to be reachable.
So how can we get ahold of you if we want to?
Email.
It's touchingearth at riseup.net.
We have a really bad-shape website, touchingearth.info.
It's out of date and we don't really know how to help it.
It's bare bones, but it has some information.
It's web design time.
I wrote some essays and put them up there.
A couple of them were published in *Turning Wheel*, a Buddhist Peace Fellowship magazine, a year or two ago.
We have another question for these folks before we close the evening.
What did you notice about being here that was helpful?
Bellingham, or this center?
Or something you liked.
**Satya:** Well, I think the most noticeable, I mentioned first Tim, but then everyone in the Sangha's openness and acceptance and interest.
The more you're living a way that at least looks on the surface different, the more you can feel isolated.
And when people reach out and are interested, it's very, very nourishing.
I've had a little more experience with it.
Fallon and Andy are a little newer to it.
It can really take a toll, especially when people are rejecting you a little bit.
So when people are really accepting and interested and want to have discussions, whether they agree or disagree, it's really wonderful.
So we've met a lot of that, both in the Sangha and also in the wider Sangha in Bellingham that we've met.
It strikes me as a nice way to, I mean, everyone has that.
That's very universal, but to make it more explicit is an interesting way to practice with that kind of energy, and that isolating yourself.
I mean, we're all weird, right?
[unclear: "Where we should go just to honor our abhors."] I just want to express my gratitude for the joy you brought and the practice that you did in Qigong with them.
The music and the food and the friendship.
You seem to exemplify the moments of joy that I've had in my life.
I see that you guys are living those moments on a daily basis.
I'm glad it seems that way.
Elvars asked us last night, "I just have this one last question."
We had it with us, and we were like, "Do you guys have any problems?"
We looked at you and said, "Nope, totally fine."
We've had a lot of really difficult times, really challenging fights and all kinds of things.
It hasn't gotten physical yet.
Thank you for speaking and visiting and practicing.

verbatim.text: Good evening everybody. Thank you for being here. So I was thinking, we've been studying for the last month or so, wisdom, Mahayana Buddhist teachings on wisdom, through the sutra and sutras on prajna paramita, which we chant about a lot as well. And one of the ways of looking at wisdom is to look at wisdom from the point of view of a sort of conventional, self-oriented basis. That often times we think about wisdom, we think about expertise, we think about doing it right, we think about avoiding embarrassment, actually. And the prajna paramita teachings seem to be suggesting there's another kind of wisdom, or a deeper wisdom, or a fuller wisdom, where the basis is not to be an expert, or to be right, or to know something. And I was thinking we have various ways to enact that in our practice, that the learning about prajna paramita is fundamentally experiential, the learning about this wisdom that doesn't have a basis in any of those things, or doesn't have a basis at all, is one of the ways this is expressed.

Wisdom with no basis whatsoever, just wisdom. And so we've talked many times about that we've inherited a somewhat complex ritual form, and that the people doing the different roles in that ritual form are not necessarily like the experts in that, which would be a rational thing from a sort of usual wisdom point of view. You would train up your best bell ringer and use him until he dies, which I guess we kind of did tonight though, because John has done this how many thousands of times? Hopefully I have a few more years. Luckily you're still making mistakes, so we're okay.

And so we put ourselves in these positions not really knowing what we're doing. And so the basis of our activity is not being the expert or getting it right, but just the doing of it. There's some richness in there, and of course psychologically that gives us various problems. We can feel anxious, we can feel self-conscious, we can feel like we don't know enough, but over time we develop a certain comfort with that. There's something comfortable about that kind of discomfort, something that's beyond our personal constricted sense of wanting to look good, or at least not look bad, wanting to blend in maybe.

These kind of roles that we have in Zen practice prevent us from blending in. Have you noticed that? They make people stick out. And it goes all the way through all the roles that we've often said. So even the person giving the talk, they're not giving the talk because they're the best trained person to give the talk. They're giving the talk because that's their job.
